message.content:
Lions (Panthera leo) and zebras (Equus quagga) are both placental mammals that belong to the clade **Laurasiatheria**—lions are in the order Carnivora, while zebras are in the order Perissodactyla.  
Their most recent common ancestor is therefore the last common ancestor of all Laurasiatherian mammals. That ancestor lived roughly 90 million years ago, during the late Cretaceous, before the diversification of the major Laurasiatherian lineages (carnivores, ungulates, cetartiodactyls, etc.). In other words, the common ancestor of lions and zebras is the ancestral Laurasiatherian mammal that gave rise to the entire clade that includes both carnivores and odd‑toed ungulates.

Or we can say the last common ancestor of all placental mammals, which lived about 100 million years ago. But more precisely, the last common ancestor of the clade Laurasiatheria.
